title: AI Studio and the Gemini API

opening.headline: Rather than just having conversations in the Gemini app, we'll look at what tools you need to create the AI functions you want.
body: The Gemini app is a ready-made chat service. You can receive an answer by entering a question, but it is difficult to create functions tailored to your needs within the app, such as a chatbot that only talks about a specific product or answers in a certain tone.

This lesson covers two entrances provided by Google. One is Google AI Studio, a web workspace for quickly experimenting with models and prompts, and the other is Gemini API, a conduit for connecting models to your applications. Let's take a look at how the two connect, and why you should handle API keys with care.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of AI Studio and Gemini API
Distinguish between app usage and API development

screens.title: What I use in the app and what I create
screens.lead: First, we look at the gap between the users of the app and the people who create it. Read the scene and think about what additional tools you might need.

visual.alt: On the left is the Gemini app conversation screen, and on the right is a speech bubble with a chatbot that only responds to our company’s products.

paragraphs: The Gemini app uses pre-built conversation features. Anyone can enter questions and receive answers. Although this approach is useful as a general-purpose chatbot, it has limitations when adapting to specific uses.

For example, let's say you want to create a customer service chatbot. This chatbot must only receive conversations related to the company's products, and must also follow a set tone. You may also need a personality that fits your purpose, such as a bot that frequently tells jokes, a bot that rhymes responses like poetry, or a bot that uses a lot of emoticons.
The questions in this lesson are simple. What tools do you need to move from app user to app creator? And how do the tools differ between the experiment stage and the service stage?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If you create a chatbot that only talks about a specific product, should the place where you first try it out and the place where you actually export it as a service be the same? You will be able to answer this question at the end of the lesson.

screens.outro: Let's start by thinking about the feature you want to create.

screens.title: What AI function would you like to create yourself?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: What AI function would you like to create yourself?
items.answer: Ideas often come from repetitive tasks, such as document summarizers, consultation chatbots, and image annotation tools. For any function, being able to say in one line what the inputs and outputs are is a good starting point.

items.prompt: Is that idea currently being used, or is it being released as a service?
items.answer: The step of confirming the idea in your head through a few conversations and the step of providing it reliably for others to use are different. In the first step, it is important to make changes quickly, and in the later steps, responsibilities such as key storage and user authentication come into play.

items.prompt: Did you think the Gemini app and Gemini API were the same thing?
items.answer: The names are similar, so it's easy to think they are the same. An app is a completed conversation service, and an API is a passage to attach a model like a part to the product you create. Check the differences between the two in detail in the following screen.

screens.outro: If you've come up with an idea, let's start with AI Studio, the first space where you can touch it lightly.

screens.title: AI Studio: A space to use models right away
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn what AI Studio's prompt screens and settings panels do.

visual.alt: AI Studio screen mockup with chat prompt screen on the left and Run settings panel on the right.

tabs.label: What is AI Studio?
tabs.body: Google AI Studio is a web workspace for quickly trying out models and experimenting with different prompts. You can talk to your model in your browser without writing a single line of code. When you see results you like, you can select Get code to get the Gemini API call code in your preferred programming language. In other words, the end of experimentation and the beginning of development follow on the same screen.

tabs.label: Chat prompt
tabs.body: AI Studio provides several prompt screens for different purposes. Among them, Chat prompt is used to create an interactive experience with multiple exchanges. On this screen, you can define the chatbot's personality by entering the role and tone of voice in System Instructions. The example in the article is the process of creating a friendly chatbot that speaks like an alien living on Jupiter's moon Europa.

tabs.label: Different prompt screens
tabs.body: In addition to Chat prompt, there are screens such as Realtime streaming and Video gen. This screen is for experiments with different purposes, such as real-time interaction or video creation. Whichever screen you choose, you can change the prompts, check the results, and adjust any settings as needed in the same way.

tabs.label: Run settings
tabs.body: The Run settings panel allows you to adjust model parameters and safety settings. You can also turn on and off tools such as structured output, function calling, code execution, and grounding. Even for the same prompt, the answer varies depending on the settings, so if the chatbot's answer is long or inconsistent, check this panel and System Instructions first.

screens.outro: If you like the results of your experiment, move it into code. Let's continue with the connection points.

screens.title: Get code and Gemini API: From experiment to service
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to step through the process of turning the prompt you created in AI Studio into calling code for your application.

visual.alt: Flow chart leading to Get code, model name, and API key on the AI Studio screen.
labels: Refine your prompt in AI Studio
Read the structure of the calling code
Identify the caller by API key

steps.title: Refine your prompt in AI Studio
steps.body: First, check the desired action using System Instructions and conversation examples in the Chat prompt. There's no code required for this step, and you can experiment with iterative changes until you're happy with the results.

steps.title: Select Get code
steps.body: When you're ready, select Get code and choose the programming language you want to use. The Gemini API overview in the documentation provides side-by-side examples of the same calls in Python, JavaScript, Java, Go, and more. Only the language is different, but the call structure is the same.

steps.title: Read the structure of the calling code
steps.body: The example code consists of three parts: Create a client, call it by passing the model name and input sentence, and then receive and use the output text. The Gemini API is the gateway to attaching text and image generation, multimodal input analysis, and conversational agent configuration to your applications.

steps.title: Identify the caller by API key
steps.body: An API key is a secret value that tells you who is calling the API. If your key is exposed, someone else can call it into your account, so you should keep it in a safe place rather than writing it down in code. The next screen takes a look at the storage locations AI Studio provides.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the structure of the calling code, let's look at where we choose which model to call and the app creation mode.

screens.title: Model list and Build mode
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare what the Models page and Build mode do for each.

states.label: Models page
states.body: The Models page lists the models available through the Gemini API and tells you the endpoint name used to call each model. This name is entered in place of the model name in the calling code. Each model has a different description, so choose the model that suits your purpose, such as inference-centered, fast processing, or voice. Even if you use the same prompt, changing the model will result in different results and speed, so it is helpful to make it a habit to write down the name of the model you chose in the code and documentation. Even if you see a new model in the list, read the description to see if it suits your purpose. The descriptions in the list are the quickest basis for comparing models.

states.label: Build mode
states.body: In Build mode, if you describe the app you want to build in a sentence, the necessary code and files will be created, and a running preview will appear on the right. A web app consists of a client (basic React) and a server (Node.js), and you can also create Android apps. You can then request corrections through chat or fix them directly in the Code tab. Secret values ​​such as API keys are stored in Secrets in Settings so that they are not revealed to the client. If you configure this value to be read only by server-side code, the key will not be passed to the user viewing the screen.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen all the tools to create a prototype, let's explain the process of moving it into a service through an example.

screens.title: Commentary: Moving Prototypes to Services
screens.lead: The instructor explains customer service chatbot cases step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: sorting out the situation
steps.body: I want to create a chatbot that only answers customer inquiries related to the company's products and uses a certain tone of voice. It is difficult to reliably specify scope and tone with general-purpose conversation apps. So, we start by checking the behavior in AI Studio.

steps.title: Step 1: Decide and repeat in Chat prompt
steps.body: Write down the chatbot's role, answer range, and tone of voice in System Instructions. For example, you could write a rule about not answering questions that are not related to your product and keep your language short and polite. Then, check the answers by entering questions that actual customers might ask several times. If there is only one instruction, the answer may be long or unruly, so be specific about the length and tone.

steps.title: Step 2: Adjust with Run settings
steps.body: If you don't like the nature of the answer, adjust the model parameters and safety settings in Run settings. If necessary, turn on tools like structured output or grounding. The purpose of this step is to have the behavior thoroughly refined before writing code.

steps.title: Step 3: Move to Get code and save the key
steps.body: When I'm satisfied with the behavior, I get the calling code with Get code and put it into my application. At this time, the API key is not written as is in the code, but is stored separately as a secret value. From this moment on, we are using the model not as an experiment, but as a part of a service.

steps.title: Step 4: Build mode if you need app form
steps.body: If you need the screen that the customer sees, describe the appearance of the chatbot app in sentences in Build mode. The screen and server are created together, and the server-side code uses the keys in Secrets, so the keys are not revealed to the client.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: This flow moves from the bench to the part. You need to be able to tell what you saw at each step so you can move on to the next step. Before exporting to a service, be sure to check that there are responsibilities such as key storage and user verification.

screens.outro: Now that we've followed the flow of the case, let's organize the boundaries between prototypes and services in a table.

screens.title: Explanation: Difference between Prototype and Service
screens.lead: Read each row of the table to compare how the AI Studio prototype differs from the Gemini API service.

data.notes: Knowing which stage you are at will make it clear what tools and responsibilities you need now. Just because the prototype works well doesn't mean it's ready for service. When moving on to service, check the items listed in the right column of this table one by one.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the difference between the two stages, we will organize the contents so far into one standard.

screens.title: Lab bench and components: organized by one standard
screens.lead: Let's summarize what we've seen so far into one perspective. As you read, think about what stage the idea you came up with is at.

paragraphs: AI Studio is the lab and Gemini API is the service part. On the bench, you can vary prompts and settings to see how your model responds. The API as a part is a conduit for repeatedly calling the results within my application.

Get code is a bridge between two worlds. The prompts from the experiment are replaced with call codes for the language of your choice. Build mode is another gateway to create the entire app with just a description, with secret values ​​placed in Secrets so they are not revealed to the client.

So the difference between writing an app and developing with an API lies in responsibilities rather than the name of the tool. App users use the completed service, but creators must solve problems such as key storage, user verification, and data storage themselves.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Talking in AI Studio does not mean creating a service, but rather confirming its possibilities. Services are a separate step complete with API calls and key management. Remembering this distinction will help me start by asking what stage I am in when choosing a tool.

glossary.def: Google's web workspace where you can quickly experiment with models and prompts and, when you like them, move them into code or apps.

This is a developer call path that connects the Gemini model to the application you are creating. It is used for generating text and images, analyzing multimodal input, and constructing conversational agents.
A secret value that identifies the party calling the API. It must be stored safely to avoid exposure.
This is AI Studio's app creation feature that generates code and files and shows a preview when you write down the app description.
This feature exports prompts created in AI Studio as calling code in the programming language of your choice.

misconceptions.myth: If you talk in AI Studio, the service will soon be created.
misconceptions.fact: AI Studio is an experiment space. Services are a separate step with elements such as API calls, key management, and user verification.

misconceptions.myth: The API key can be written as is in the code.
misconceptions.fact: An API key is a secret value that identifies the caller. Place it in an archiving function such as Secrets in Settings so that it is not exposed to the client.

misconceptions.myth: The Gemini app and Gemini API are the same thing.
misconceptions.fact: An app is a completed conversation service, and an API is a part attached to your product. The roles and responsibilities of the writer are different.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: AI Studio is a lab for experimenting with prompts and models.
Gemini API is a component that attaches the results of experiments to my service.
Get code connects the two, and the API key is a secret value that identifies the caller, so keep it safe.
Prototypes and services have different purposes and responsibilities.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Is the AI feature I came up with currently in the prototype or service stage?

checks.q: I created a prompt I liked in AI Studio. What should I do first to call this from my app?
options: Select Get code to receive the calling code for the desired language.
Copy the conversation history from the Gemini app and paste it into the app.
Turn off all safety settings in Run settings and run again.
Just memorize the endpoint name on the Models page.
checks.explain: Get code serves as a bridge that turns AI Studio's experiment results into Gemini API call code. You can also choose a language from Python, JavaScript, etc.

wrong.1: The conversation history is not a calling code, so it is not a conduit for the app to call the model.
wrong.2: Safety settings are adjustments to model behavior, not steps to move into code.
wrong.3: The model name is just one element in the code and does not constitute a call by itself.

checks.intro: Check out for yourself the flow you just saw. Results are not recorded, and commentary appears immediately after you select an option.

checks.explain: Models lists models, Build creates an app based on descriptions, Secrets stores keys, and Run settings adjusts parameters and tools.
checks.intro: Match the roles of screens and functions. Results are not recorded.

Receive the code with Get code and keep the API key as a secret value.
If you need an app form, create the screen and server together in Build mode.
